reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
clinicalPearls: Most are squamous cell carcinomas and arise through two main routes: an HPV-associated pathway seen in younger women and an HPV-independent pathway linked to lichen sclerosus and chronic inflammation in older women

It commonly presents as persistent vulvar itching, a lump, ulcer, or plaque, sometimes with bleeding, pain, or discharge, and diagnosis is often delayed by patient reluctance and repeated empirical treatment
Any persistent or atypical vulvar lesion should undergo biopsy rather than prolonged treatment for presumed dermatitis or infection
Spread occurs predominantly to inguinofemoral lymph nodes, so accurate groin node assessment is critical to staging and prognosis
Sentinel lymph node biopsy is used in selected early tumours to reduce the morbidity of full inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy
Surgery is the mainstay for localised disease, with wide local excision or vulvectomy and appropriate groin node management guided by tumour depth and size
Radiotherapy, often combined with chemotherapy, is used for advanced disease, positive nodes, or to preserve function and reduce the extent of surgery
Precursor vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia and lichen sclerosus warrant surveillance because of their malignant potential
reference.pathophysiology: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma develops from the vulvar epithelium by two principal mechanisms. In younger women, persistent high-risk human papillomavirus infection drives usual-type vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia that can progress to invasive cancer. In older women, chronic dermatological conditions such as lichen sclerosus produce differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia and HPV-independent carcinoma. Invasive tumour infiltrates local structures and spreads first to superficial and deep inguinofemoral nodes and subsequently to pelvic nodes, with distant metastasis occurring late.
additionalDifferentials: Vulvar melanoma, Paget disease, or basal cell carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy of the vulvar lesion for histological diagnosis and depth of invasion
Examination of the inguinal regions and vulva under adequate visualisation, with colposcopy where indicated
Pelvic MRI to assess local extent and nodal involvement
CT or PET-CT for regional and distant staging
Sentinel lymph node evaluation in appropriately selected early-stage tumours
redFlags: A persistent vulvar lump, ulcer, or plaque that does not resolve with treatment
Chronic vulvar itching or bleeding in an older woman with lichen sclerosus
Palpable or fixed inguinal lymph nodes
Rapidly enlarging or ulcerating vulvar lesion
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is largely determined by inguinofemoral nodal status and tumour stage; node-negative localised disease has good survival after surgery, whereas nodal involvement or advanced local spread substantially reduces outcomes.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating a persistent vulvar lesion as dermatitis or thrush without biopsy
Failing to assess and manage inguinal lymph nodes appropriately
Neglecting surveillance of lichen sclerosus and vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia
Underestimating the psychosexual and functional impact when planning surgery
references: DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
management: High-grade VIN (HSIL) is generally managed with excision rather than ablation, since excision can uncover unsuspected invasive disease; topical imiquimod is a preferred first-line medical option for recurrent HSIL
Small, early-stage invasive lesions confined to the vulva can be managed with radical local excision alone when stromal invasion is minimal
Larger T2 lesions are managed with wide local excision or modified radical vulvectomy, addressing the primary tumor and inguinal nodes through separate incisions to reduce morbidity
Locally advanced disease may require radical surgery up to pelvic exenteration, concurrent chemoradiation, or a combination, chosen based on the likelihood of clear margins without exenteration
Positive margins should prompt consideration of re-excision; close margins alone can be managed with observation or postoperative radiotherapy

Adjuvant radiotherapy is recommended after surgery for early-stage disease with high-risk features such as nodal involvement, close or positive margins, larger tumor size, or lymphovascular invasion, and should not be unduly delayed
Sentinel lymph node biopsy is the standard nodal staging approach for appropriately selected early-stage, node-negative patients, reducing morbidity compared with full inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy
Full inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy or bilateral sentinel biopsy is used when a sentinel node cannot be identified or bilateral drainage is uncertain

Nodal management after sentinel biopsy is risk-stratified by metastasis size, with radiotherapy alone considered for isolated tumor cells or micrometastases and lymphadenectomy generally used for macrometastases
Adjuvant nodal radiotherapy is indicated after lymphadenectomy for multiple positive nodes, a fixed or ulcerated node, or extranodal extension

Bulky or locally advanced disease is treated with concurrent platinum-based chemoradiation, using intensity-modulated radiotherapy to spare surrounding organs, given either preoperatively or as definitive treatment

Recurrent or metastatic disease may be treated with platinum-based chemotherapy combinations, PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy in HPV-positive disease, or bevacizumab-containing regimens extrapolated from cervical cancer

Vulvovaginal melanoma is managed separately from squamous cell vulvar cancer with wide local excision, generally avoiding morbid surgery, and consideration of KIT or MAPK-pathway targeted therapy if KIT-mutated and unresectable

Any invasive vulvar lesion or concerning high-grade VIN warrants referral to gynecologic oncology, with radiation oncology and multidisciplinary chemoradiation planning involved for node-positive, locally advanced, or margin-positive disease
